newsitem.title: ITALY: Italian govt intervenes in metalworkers' dispute.
newsitem.headline: Italian govt intervenes in metalworkers' dispute.

text.p: The Italian government has put forward a compromise deal in the long-running metalworkers' pay dispute, a move welcomed by trade unions but given a cool reception by management.

Unions representing some 1.7 million metal and engineering workers have already held two one-day stoppages to press their claim for higher wages and have threatened to widen the strike action to other sectors unless their demands were met.
Talks aimed at resolving the six-month old dispute broke down last week and supporters of the centre-left government urged Prime Minister Romano Prodi to intervene.

Bowing to the pressure, Labour Minister Tiziano Treu said in a letter late on Saturday that management should offer workers a pay rise of 200,000 lire ($130) a month for the 1996-1998 contract period.
In addition, he promised tax breaks for firms in the under-developed south of Italy.
Unions had been asking for a monthly pay increase of 230,000 lire while management had offered 139,000 lire.
"This offer seems fair and I hope it will help get the negotiations going again," Sergio Cofferati, leader of Italy's largest union, the Cigl, told newspaper Corriere della Sera.
Employers, who have recently grown highly critical of Prodi's seven-month old government, were less impressed.
"It would be very difficult to accept this proposal," Michele Figurati, director general of employers' federation Federmeccanica, said in an interview with La Stampa daily.
"It seems strange that the government should come up with exact figures. I think it is an interference in private negotiations," he added.
However both sides said they would examine the proposals in more detail, with the unions due to meet later on Sunday.

Contracts in the metalworkers' sector, which accounts for about 40 percent of total manufacturing output in Italy, expired in June, and differences between management and unions have widened rather than narrowed in the subsequent negotiations.
At the heart of the quarrel lies a landmark 1993 wage accord which scrapped automatic index-linked salary increases.
Unions say the accord allows for full reimbursement for higher-than-expected inflation in the past contractural period. Managers disagree.

The metalworkers' pay deal will set the standard for wage rounds under discussion in a number of other industrial sectors, and many groups, including the Bank of Italy and International Monetary Fund (IMF), have urged constraint on the unions in the fear that a high settlement might set off inflation.
However the unions said the government had now vindicated their interpretation of the 1993 labour deal.

"Everyone has been telling us we have taken the wrong position, but the government proposals show we weren't mistaken," Gianni Italia, head of the FIM-CISL union, told La Stampa newspaper on Sunday. $1 = 1,525 lire
